question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a comfortable stair with the lowest energy requirement, a standard design rule combines riser height r and tread depth t, based on the stride length of an adult. Within what range should 2r + t lie?
source: In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.
context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. From the physiological point of view, the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.

answer.text:
The standard German stair formula (Schrittmaßregel) is 2r + t = 59–65 cm, with 63 cm as the typical stride length of an adult. For example, r = 17 cm and t = 29 cm gives 63 cm.

Answer: A

question.text: Under the German Energy Saving Ordinance EnEV 2007 (envelope area process), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand of a building is determined as a function of which building-geometry ratio?
options: Built-up area to total plot area (plot coverage ratio)
Heat-transmitting envelope area to heated building volume (A/Ve)
Heated net floor area to gross building volume (NFA/V)
Glazed façade area to total external wall area (window ratio)
source: Depending on the ratio of heat-transmitting area A to heated building volumes V_e (A/V_e ratio), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand will be determined according to EnEV 2007, according to the envelope area process.
context: Depending on the ratio of heat-transmitting area A to heated building volumes V_e (A/V_e ratio), the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand will be determined according to EnEV 2007, according to the envelope area process. The basis for this is the monthly balance procedure (DIN EN 832) with the conditions given in DIN 4108.

answer.text:
Under EnEV 2007, the maximum permissible annual primary energy demand of a building is determined from the compactness of the building, expressed as the ratio of the heat-transmitting envelope area A to the enclosed heated building volume Ve (A/Ve). The reference values in the annex tables are tied to this ratio. For residential buildings the maximum is also expressed as a function of A/Ve, and the useful area AN is calculated from Ve.

Answer: B

options: External dimensions of all storeys including basements, balconies and terraces
Ground-floor footprint only, including garages and their access
External dimensions of all full storeys, excluding balconies, loggias and terraces
Net internal floor area of all storeys, including balconies and loggias

context:
Measures of building use → 1

answer.text:
Under BauNVO §20 (Abs. 3), the floor area is determined from the external dimensions of the building in all storeys. Only full storeys (Vollgeschosse) count under the older rule, and balconies, loggias and terraces are not included, along with certain other elements.

Option C matches this. Option A is wrong because it includes balconies and terraces and counts basements, and the other options describe different measures altogether. B describes the ground-floor footprint, which is not the GFZ measure. D uses net internal area, which is not what the regulation says.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) planning guidance on parking for private houses, which form of car shelter (other than an enclosed garage) is described as cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics because it avoids condensation in cold cars in winter, and space-saving?
source: In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics
context: Space requirement → 7 – 12. A reduction in the parking area is possible for private houses. The tendency of modern cars to get larger (including in height) should be taken into account.

In addition to garages, roofed-over parking places (carports) represent a cheaper, more beneficial in terms of building physics (no condensation in cold cars in the winter!) and space-saving possibility for protecting cars adequately from the weather (a close wall on the weather side is a good idea). A combination with enclosed storerooms (for bicycles etc.) is to be recommended → 11. Carports are particularly suitable for communal parking places → 12.

answer.text:
The question is about German planning guidance (Neufert-style) on parking at private houses. The alternative to an enclosed garage is the carport, which is cheaper. It is also better for building physics because a cold car does not bring condensation into a warm closed garage in winter, and it saves space.

Of the options, only the open carport is a car shelter other than an enclosed garage that fits this description.

Answer: B

question.text: According to the German high-rise building regulations: (a) above what height of the uppermost floor (on one side of the building, above ground level) does a building intended for long-term human occupation count as a high-rise building, and (b) what minimum walking width must each of the emergency stairs have in a high-rise building up to 60 m high?
source: High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m.
context:
Definition of high-rise buildings
High-rise buildings are those intended for long-term human occupation whose upper-most floor on one side of the building is more than 22 m above ground level.

Stairs
High-rise buildings up to 60 m high: at least two emergency stairs must be available, which must be located opposite in two separate fire compartments. Their walking width must be at least 1.25 m. The wellhole must be min. 0.80 m wide in order to avoid having to lay hoses on the stairs. Smoke outlets must be provided at their highest point (5% of the floor area but min. 1 m^2). The exit must be directly into the open air or through a lobby without any fire load. In exceptional cases, one staircase can be approved for high-rise buildings up to 60 m in height, if it is a safety staircase. Requirements for the location of stairs → 2 – 5.

answer.text:
In Germany, the Musterbauordnung (MBO) defines a high-rise (Hochhaus) as a building where the floor of at least one occupancy room (Aufenthaltsraum) lies more than 22 m above ground level.

For the stair width, the Muster-Hochhausrichtlinie (MHHR) requires safety stairwells (notwendige Treppen) to have a minimum usable width of 1.25 m. Under the MBO, the usable width of required stairs is set by the building's use, but the high-rise guideline sets 1.25 m. Some sources say that in high-rises up to 60 m, the stair width is 1.25 m, and above 60 m it must be 1.50 m or more. In this case, 1.25 m fits the "up to 60 m" condition.

The 22 m threshold and the 1.25 m width therefore match option B.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: From a physiological point of view, at what stair pitch and what riser-to-tread ratio (r/t, in cm) is 'climbing effort' generally considered to be used best?
source: the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29.
context: The experience of using stairs and access routes is very varied: from the creative possibilities of the most diverse residential stairs to an elaborate outside staircase, which one can stride up and down. Climbing stairs takes on average seven times the energy input as walking on the flat. From the physiological point of view, the best use of 'climbing effort' is at a stair pitch of 30° and a ratio of riser (r) to tread (t) of 17/29. The pitch is determined by the stride length of an adult (approx. 59–65 cm). In order to determine a suitable pitch with the lowest energy requirement, this formula applies: 2 r + t = 59–65 cm.

answer.text:
The Schrittmaßregel (stride rule) is 2s + t = 59–65 cm, which gives the ideal stair at about 17/29 with a 30° pitch. The 17/29 ratio checks out: 2×17 + 29 = 63 cm, which is within the range. The Neufert figure for the ideal stair is also 17/29, with an angle of about 30°.

Checking the other options against the same rule:
- A: 2×15 + 32 = 62, which fits, but the pitch is 25° and the comfort is less than the physiological optimum.
- B: 2×19 + 26 = 64, which also fits, but the pitch is steeper at about 36°.
- D: 2×20 + 24 = 64, but this stair is steep.

Several options satisfy the rule, but the physiologically best use of climbing effort is the 30° stair at 17/29, since 17/29 is the standard ideal stair.

Answer: C

answer.text:
DIN 18065 sets the minimum usable stair width for residential buildings with up to two flats at 0.80 m. The same standard gives the tread/riser ratio as 17/28 (riser 14–19 cm, going at least 24 cm, and the stair rule 2s + g = 59–65 cm). answer.text:
The German Muster-Garagenverordnung (MGarVO) §4 sets minimum parking space dimensions, and the figures depend on the type of use:

- Garages with a frequently changing user group (e.g. public, shopping): 2.50 m wide (the width is 3.50 m for spaces for wheelchair users).
- Garages used by a regular group of users (e.g. residents, employees): 2.30 m wide. In the older version the figure was 2.30 m.

Several Länder regulations (GarVO) state:
- Stellplätze: 5.0 m long and at least 2.30 m wide.
- With 2.50 m for spaces in garages with frequent changes in users, per the Garagenverordnung.

Stairs must have handrails on both sides, which are to be continued past landings and window openings and past the last steps. The stairs must have solid risers. Corridors and entrance halls must be at least 1.50 m wide. One toilet must also be suitable and accessible for wheelchair users; this is to be indicated by a sign.

Movement areas
Are those necessary for moving a wheelchair and are to be designed according to the minimum space requirement of a wheelchair user. The wheelchair → ① – ④ and the movement area for the person → ⑨ – ⑫ provide the modules for this. The dimensions of the movement area are 0.90–1.80 m and may overlap – except in front of lift doors. A depth and width of at least 1.50 m should be provided in every room for turning. (More information on movement areas is found on the following pages.)

answer.text:
DIN 18040-1 and -2 require a wheelchair turning space ("Bewegungsfläche") of 1.50 m × 1.50 m. This is the standard figure for turning in place, and it is expected in rooms and in front of fixtures.

The other options do not match this requirement. Dimensions of 1.40 × 1.70 m do appear in German guidance, but for other uses (for example, the elevator cabin size under DIN EN 81-70). 1.20 m is a path width, not a turning space. 1.80 m is the older or international figure.

Answer: C

question.text: In barrier-free public buildings per German guidance, (a) how many wheelchair-accessible toilets must be provided in sanitary facilities, and (b) in which direction must doors to toilets, showers and changing rooms open?

Two in each sanitary facility; doors open outward
One per building; sliding doors only
At least one in all sanitary facilities; doors open inward
source: At least one toilet must be provided for wheelchair users in all sanitary facilities.
Doors to toilets, showers and changing rooms must open outward.

Doors
Clear passage width of doors \( \geq 0.90 \) m \( \rightarrow \) \( ① + ② \). Doors to toilets, showers and changing rooms must open outward.

Sanitary facilities
At least one toilet must be provided for wheelchair users in all sanitary facilities. The seat height should be 48 cm → 8.

answer.text:
This follows DIN 18040-1 (barrier-free public buildings) and the Neufert guidance based on it.

(a) DIN 18040-1 requires at least one wheelchair-accessible toilet in each sanitary facility, so "at least one in all sanitary facilities" fits. The requirement is not one per building, and it is not two per facility.

(b) Doors to toilets, showers and changing rooms must open outward, so that a person who has fallen inside cannot block the door. Sliding doors are also permitted, but the guidance does not limit the options to sliding doors only.

Option A matches both points.

question.text: According to the German model building regulations (MBO), what clear opening width must the front doors of flats that are accessed by lifts have (for wheelchair access)?
source: front doors of flats which are accessed by lifts must have a clear opening width of 90 cm (for wheelchair access). The door height in this case should be at least 2.10 m.
context: According to the MBO, front doors of flats which are accessed by lifts must have a clear opening width of 90 cm (for wheelchair access). The door height in this case should be at least 2.10 m. Door thresholds are to be avoided. The entrance door must also comply with acoustic and fire protection requirements.

answer.text:
Recalling the relevant rule is difficult. MBO § 39 covers lifts, and § 50 covers barrier-free construction. Under § 50, flats must be accessible for wheelchair users, and the DIN 18040-2 requirement is a clear width of 90 cm for doors.

The question asks about "front doors of flats that are accessed by lifts." This appears to come from a list of architectural design rules, possibly Neufert. In Neufert's treatment of the MBO, lifts are required in buildings with more than 5 floors, and the rule is likely "Wohnungseingangstüren ... lichte Breite 90 cm".

In the older MBO, § 39 (4) says that lifts must have a floor area of 1.10 m × 2.10 m, and the door width must be 0.90 m. The MBO also says that doors to flats accessible by lift must have a clear width of at least 0.90 m. DIN 18025-2 required 90 cm for doors, while DIN 18040 requires 90 cm for barrier-free doors, with 80 cm in some cases. The MBO's § 39 (4) states: "Zu den Aufzügen muss ein Zugang mit lichter Breite von mindestens 0,90 m". On balance, 90 cm seems most likely.

question.text: In barrier-free design per German guidance, what minimum clear internal dimensions (width × depth) must a lift car have?

question.text: Under the German model building regulations (MBO), what accessibility requirement applies to residential buildings with more than two flats?
options: At least 10% of the flats must be accessible, with every room wheelchair-usable
Flats on one floor must have a step-free entrance, but no room inside need be wheelchair-usable
Flats on one floor must be accessible, with living rooms, bedrooms, a WC, a bathroom and the kitchen wheelchair-usable
All flats on every floor must be accessible, with every room wheelchair-usable
source: In buildings with more than two flats, the flats on one floor must be accessible.

In buildings with more than two flats, the flats on one floor must be accessible. In these flats, the living rooms and bedrooms, one toilet, one bathroom and the kitchen or kitchenette must be accessible with a wheelchair.

answer.text:
MBO §50(1): In buildings with more than two flats, the flats of one floor must be accessible (barrierefrei erreichbar). In these flats, living rooms and bedrooms, a toilet, a bathroom, a kitchen or cooking area must be accessible barrier-free (the older version said "mit dem Rollstuhl zugänglich"). question.text: In barrier-free design per German guidance, beyond what corridor length must a passing place for two wheelchair users be provided, and what minimum size (width and depth) must it have?
source: Corridors and routes longer than 15 m must have a passing place for two wheelchair users of at least 1.80 m width and depth.
context:
Corridors and meeting areas
Corridors and routes longer than 15 m must have a passing place for two wheelchair users of at least 1.80 m width and depth.

answer.text:
This question appears to refer to the German DIN 18040 or the related guidance on barrier-free construction. I am recalling this from memory rather than from a checked source.

In DIN 18040-1, a corridor should be at least 1.50 m wide. For long corridors, a passing place is required so that two wheelchair users can pass each other. I do not recall the exact numbers with certainty, but the relevant wording is probably the Neufert-style rule that where corridors are longer than 15 m, a passing place of 1.80 m × 1.80 m is needed.

Other sources give different figures. The Austrian ÖNORM B 1600 specifies 2.00 m width for a passing place. Some German sources state "Begegnungsflächen 1,80 m × 1,80 m" for corridors longer than 15 m. I cannot confirm that precisely, but it seems the most consistent with what I remember, so I will go with it.

question.text: In barrier-free design per German guidance, what minimum width must the movement area next to the top and bottom of stairs have, and is the tread of the first step counted as part of it?
source: The movement area next to the stairs going up and down must be min. 1.50 m wide; the tread of the first step is not to be included in the calculation of the movement area
context: Stairs. The movement area next to the stairs going up and down must be min. 1.50 m wide; the tread of the first step is not to be included in the calculation of the movement area → 7.

answer.text:
DIN 18040-1 and the "Bewegungsflächen" rules: for stairs, there is a requirement that at the beginning and end of stairs, a movement area of at least 1.50 m is needed. I'm not certain whether the first step's tread is counted.

For ramps, DIN 18040-1 specifies a movement area of 1.50 m × 1.50 m at the start and end of ramps. For stairs, the accessibility guidance (e.g., Barrierefreies Bauen, Neufert) says: "Vor und hinter Treppen sind Bewegungsflächen von mind. 1,50 m Tiefe anzuordnen"? In many guidance texts on stair design (the BayBO or Bauordnung guidance), "Der Treppenauftritt der ersten Stufe wird nicht auf die Bewegungsfläche angerechnet" seems plausible, since the tread of a step is not level ground. I recall that for DIN 18065, the "Treppenabsatz" is counted differently. In the Neufert text: "Bewegungsfläche 1.50 m, Stufenauftritt nicht mitgerechnet."

I'll go with D.

question.text: In barrier-free design per German guidance, what minimum depth of movement area must be provided next to the long side of a wheelchair user's vehicle in a car park?
source:
min. 1.50 m deep ...
in front of therapy facilities (e.g. bath, couch), in front of wheelchair parking places, next to the long side of the vehicle of a wheelchair user in car parks
context:
min. 1.50 m deep ...
in front of therapy facilities (e.g. bath, couch), in front of wheelchair parking places, next to the long side of the vehicle of a wheelchair user in car parks → p. 23 ⑩.

answer.text:
The relevant German standard is DIN 18040-1 (public buildings) and DIN 18040-2 for housing.

Under DIN 18040-1, parking spaces for wheelchair users are 3.50 m wide and 5.00 m long. They can also be 2.50 m wide with a 1.00 m movement area at the side.

The question asks for the depth of the movement area next to the long side of the vehicle. DIN 18040-1 says movement areas next to the long side of vehicles must be at least 1.50 m wide, and 1.50 m is also the figure that appears in the Neufert-type guidance. The 3.50 m total width is the 2.50 m vehicle plus a 1.00 m strip, but that is the older combined dimension.

The 1.50 m movement area is stated for parking in the standard's section on car parks in a general sense. For parking, DIN 18040-1 gives 3.50 m width × 5.00 m length, and DIN 18040-2 calls for 3.50 m width as well. In DIN 18040-1, the 1.50 m is given as the movement area at the side and rear.

The older DIN 18024-1 required a 3.50 m width. In the newer standards, "Bewegungsflächen" next to the long side must be 1.50 m, and 1.20 m is the figure for the rear of the vehicle. Based on this, I settle on 1.50 m.

Answer: C

question.text: Under the German building rules for normal (non-high-rise) buildings, what is the maximum distance from every location in inhabited rooms and basements to the stairwell of at least one legally essential stairway or to an exit?
source: Every location in inhabited rooms and basements must be \( \leq 35 \) m from the stairwell of at least one legally essential stairway or exit.
context: Every location in inhabited rooms and basements must be \( \leq 35 \) m from the stairwell of at least one legally essential stairway or exit. If a number of stairways are necessary, then they should be arranged so that the escape route is as short as possible. Any openings from stairwells into cellars, uninhabited roof spaces, workshops, shops, storerooms, and similar must be fitted with self-closing doors with a fire resistance rating of 30 minutes.

answer.text:
This question appears to track the Musterbauordnung (MBO) §35 on stairways. It states that from every point of a habitable room (Aufenthaltsraum) there must be a stairwell of at least one required stairway (notwendige Treppe) or an exit to the outdoors within a maximum of 35 m.

The 35 m limit applies to Aufenthaltsräume and basement rooms. In the MBO, the second sentence of §35(2) reads: "Von jeder Stelle eines Aufenthaltsraumes sowie eines Kellergeschosses muss mindestens ein Treppenraum einer notwendigen Treppe oder ein Ausgang ins Freie in höchstens 35 m Entfernung erreichbar sein." The 40 m figure belongs to the Muster-Verkaufsstättenverordnung or similar rules, while 25 m is used in other contexts, such as industrial buildings.

Answer: A

question.text: In wheelchair-accessible dwellings per German guidance, what should be the minimum floor area of a living room with an eating area in a flat for one person and in a flat for 2–4 people, and what minimum room width applies for a 1–2 person household?

question.text: Under German building regulations, how many independent escape routes to the open air must a residential or commercial unit with at least one occupied room have on each storey, and if the unit is not at ground level, what may the second escape route be?
options: At least two; the second via a second essential stair or a point reachable by fire brigade rescue equipment
At least two; both must run via separate legally essential staircases in their own stairwells
One; a second is required only for units more than 22 m above ground
At least two; the second must be an external escape stair fixed to the façade
source: Residential or commercial units with at least one occupied room must have at least two independent escape routes leading to the open air on each storey.
the second escape route via a second essential staircase or a single unified location which is accessible with the rescue equipment of the local fire brigade
context:
Escape routes
Residential or commercial units with at least one occupied room must have at least two independent escape routes leading to the open air on each storey. (If the units are not at ground level, the first escape route must be via a legally essential staircase, if required in its own (legally essential) stairwell, and the second escape route via a second essential staircase or a single unified location which is accessible with the rescue equipment of the local fire brigade → 3. From every location in an occupied room, there must be within max. 35 m at least one exit into a legally essential stairwell or into the open air → 4. A second escape route is not required if escape is via a safety stairwell → 5, into which fire and smoke cannot penetrate due to the provision of 'fire balconies' or safety vestibules with forced ventilation → p. 246 High-rise buildings.

Escape routes
Residential or commercial units with at least one occupied room must have at least two independent escape routes leading to the open air on each storey. (If the units are not at ground level, the first escape route must be via a legally essential staircase, if required in its own (legally essential) stairwell, and the second escape route via a second essential staircase or a single unified location which is accessible with the rescue equipment of the local fire brigade → 3. From every location in an occupied room, there must be within max. 35 m at least one exit into a legally essential stairwell or into the open air → 4. A second escape route is not required if escape is via a safety stairwell → 5, into which fire and smoke cannot penetrate due to the provision of 'fire balconies' or safety vestibules with forced ventilation → p. 246 High-rise buildings.

answer.text:
This matches the Musterbauordnung (MBO) § 33. Every usable unit with at least one occupied room (Aufenthaltsraum), such as a dwelling, office or practice, must have two independent escape routes to the open air on each storey. The first escape route must lead via a necessary staircase. The second may be a second necessary staircase, or an access point that the fire brigade can reach with rescue equipment (for example a window reachable by a ladder). A second staircase is not required if rescue via a safe stairwell (Sicherheitstreppenraum) is possible.

Option B is wrong because it demands two staircases, when the rule allows fire brigade rescue equipment as the second route. Option C is wrong because the two-route requirement applies in general, not only above 22 m. Option D is wrong because it does not require an external stair.

Answer: A

This looks like it comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, which gives the rule for escape routes and exits as 1.0 m of width per 150 people. The Versammlungsstättenverordnung (MVStättV) gives a different figure: 1.2 m per 200 people. That is a related rule but not the one I am recalling.

For restaurants specifically, I recall Neufert saying that "Ausgänge und Notausgänge... 1,0 m breit je 150 Personen". I am recalling this from memory, not checking it against a source.

The other options (100, 200, 250) fit other regulations less well. The 1.2 m per 200 people figure would be for assembly venues, so 150 is the best match for the restaurant guidance.

question.text: In wheelchair-accessible dwellings per German guidance, what minimum width must the movement area have between walls within the dwelling and along routes within the house?
source:
min. 1.20 m wide…
along furniture which the wheelchair user approaches from the side, along the access side of a non-wheelchair user’s bed → 9, between walls within the dwelling
context:
min. 1.20 m wide…
along furniture which the wheelchair user approaches from the side, along the access side of a non-wheelchair user’s bed → 9, between walls within the dwelling, next to operated equipment → p. 22 9, between wheel kerbs of a ramp → p. 22 3 and on routes within a house.

meta.title: 无障碍住宅的户内活动区宽度

answer.text:
DIN 18040-2 (barrier-free building, housing) distinguishes between "R" (wheelchair-accessible) and basic accessibility. For R dwellings, the movement area is 1.50 m x 1.50 m, and the minimum width of movement areas along walls and on routes is 1.20 m. Corridors in the dwelling must be 1.20 m wide for R, and 1.50 m is the turning space.

The question asks for "minimum width of movement area between walls within the dwelling and along routes within the house." DIN 18040-2 section 5.2: "Bewegungsflächen... Die Bewegungsfläche muss mindestens 1,50 m × 1,50 m... Bewegungsflächen entlang der Wege, 1,20 m breit". Basic accessibility requires 1.20 m for the width of movement areas between walls, and for R it is 1.20 m as well. Specifically, "Die Breite von Bewegungsflächen zwischen Wänden... 1,20 m" and "Flure 1,20 m".

Some versions state 1.50 m for the movement area between walls (e.g., in the Austrian ÖNORM or the state building codes). In the DIN, 5.2 reads "Die Bewegungsfläche... Wege... Breite 1,20 m, bei Richtungswechsel 1,50 m." So the answer is 1.20 m.

question.text: Under German building regulations for stairs, how must all main staircases be enclosed?
options: In a stairwell enclosed on the lowest storeys only, the upper flights may be open galleries
In a stairwell enclosed only above the ground floor, opening freely into the entrance hall
In a continuous stairwell that, with its access routes and exit to the open air, can safely be used for escape
No enclosure is needed if the whole building is fitted with a sprinkler system
source: All main staircases must be enclosed in a continuous stairwell, which is designed and arranged so that, including its access routes and exit to the open air, it can safely be used for escape.
context: For determining the dimensions and form of stairs, their overall functional and design purpose is just as important as the relationships described above. Not just changing level is important, but how the level is changed. For outside stairs, low steps are preferable, with dimensions of 12 × 41 to 16 × 30 cm. Stairs in offices or emergency stairs should, in contrast, make it possible to change level quickly. All main staircases must be enclosed in a continuous stairwell, which is designed and arranged so that, including its access routes and exit to the open air, it can safely be used for escape. Exit width should be \( \leq \) stair width.

meta.title: 主楼梯须设在连续封闭的楼梯间

answer.text:
German building regulations (the Musterbauordnung and the state building codes) require that every main staircase (notwendige Treppe) be located in a stairwell, called a Treppenraum. The stairwell has to be continuous, meaning it runs without interruption from the lowest to the highest storey. Together with its access routes and its exit to the open air, it must allow safe use as an escape route. This matches option C.

Answer: C

question.text: In wheelchair-accessible dwellings per German guidance, what minimum movement area (width × depth) is required to one side of the WC, and what minimum distance is required from the other side of the WC to the wall or furniture?
source: The movement area to the right or left of the WC must be at least 95 cm wide and 70 cm deep. From one side of the WC towards the wall, or furniture, there must be a distance of min. 30 cm
context:
Bathroom
The bathroom is to be provided with a wheelchair-accessible shower. The later installation of a bath should be possible near the shower. The movement area to the right or left of the WC must be at least 95 cm wide and 70 cm deep. From one side of the WC towards the wall, or furniture, there must be a distance of min. 30 cm → 2 – 4. No bathroom doors may open inwards.

Bathroom
The bathroom is to be provided with a wheelchair-accessible shower. The later installation of a bath should be possible near the shower. The movement area to the right or left of the WC must be at least 95 cm wide and 70 cm deep. From one side of the WC towards the wall, or furniture, there must be a distance of min. 30 cm → 2 – 4. min. 1.50 m wide and min. 1.50 m deep...
a turning place in every room (excepting small rooms, which the wheelchair user can use by moving backwards and forwards), the shower → ① + ④, in front of the WC and vanity unit → ② – ④, in an outside seating area, in front of lift shaft doors, at the start and end of a ramp and in front of the intake of a rubbish chute.

answer.text:
This appears to come from DIN 18040-2 (barrier-free dwellings), with the R (wheelchair) variant. For the WC, the standard requires a movement area of at least 90 cm wide and 150 cm deep in front of it, and for R-dwellings a lateral transfer space is required.

For R-dwellings, the standard says: "Neben dem WC-Becken ist beidseitig ein Abstand von mindestens 30 cm zu Wänden oder Einrichtungsgegenständen erforderlich. Auf einer Seite ist eine Bewegungsfläche von mindestens 90 cm Breite und 70 cm Tiefe erforderlich." That is the standard for accessible dwellings.

The question asks for the movement area to one side of the WC and the minimum distance on the other side. Per DIN 18040-2 for wheelchair use, the movement area is 90 cm wide × 70 cm deep on one side, and 30 cm distance on the other side. For the general accessible (non-R) case, the distance is 20 cm on both sides. No option combines 90 × 70 with 30 cm, but option B gives 90 × 70 with 20 cm. 

The options are: A 80×60/25; B 90×70/20; C 95×70/30; D 120×70/30.

In DIN 18040-2, section 5.5.3: "Neben dem WC-Becken muss auf einer Seite eine Bewegungsfläche von mindestens 90 cm Breite und 70 cm Tiefe vorhanden sein... auf der anderen Seite ein Abstand von mindestens 30 cm zur Wand oder zu Einrichtungsgegenständen." Another version: the movement area is 95 cm wide for the R-variant (DIN 18040-2 R requires 95 cm wide × 70 cm deep, with 30 cm on the other side), and the 90 cm figure refers to the non-R variant with the 20 cm distance. I recall that in DIN 18040-2 the WC requires "Bewegungsfläche 90 cm breit, 70 cm tief" on one side, and 30 cm on the other side, for the base standard. Since option C pairs 95 × 70 with 30, and the question specifies "wheelchair-accessible," I recall the R-requirement reads "seitlich 95 cm breit und 70 cm tief", which matches C.

Answer: C

question.text: Under the German model building regulations (MBO), into fire compartments of what maximum length must larger buildings be sub-divided by fire compartment walls, and what fire resistance classification must these walls have?
source: to sub-divide larger buildings into fire compartments of not more than 40 m.
Fire compartment walls must be fireproof, structurally stable when exposed to fire and consist of non-combustible materials (F 90A).
context: According to the MBO, fire compartment walls are to be constructed in the following locations: the external walls of buildings, when the wall is less than 2.50 m from the plot boundary; between terraced buildings on the same plot boundary; and to sub-divide larger buildings into fire compartments of not more than 40 m.

Fire compartment walls must be fireproof, structurally stable when exposed to fire and consist of non-combustible materials (F 90A). They must normally extend continuously from the foundations to min. 30 cm above the roof (min. 50 cm for a soft roof covering and in industrial buildings) or be capped with a projecting slab → 6. For low buildings, they must continue to immediately under the roof covering. Cables and pipes which penetrate fire compartment walls must have a 90 min fire resistance class. Openings in fire compartment walls are generally impermissible. They can be allowed through fire compartment walls within buildings and then have to be provided with fireproof self-closing doors (T 90 door or gate) → p. 512 2.

Fire compartment walls must be fireproof, structurally stable when exposed to fire and consist of non-combustible materials (F 90A). They must normally extend continuously from the foundations to min. 30 cm above the roof (min. 50 cm for a soft roof covering and in industrial buildings) or be capped with a projecting slab → 6. For low buildings, they must continue to immediately under the roof covering. Cables and pipes which penetrate fire compartment walls must have a 90 min fire resistance class. Openings in fire compartment walls are generally impermissible. They can be allowed through fire compartment walls within buildings and then have to be provided with fireproof self-closing doors (T 90 door or gate) → p. 512 2.

answer.text:
MBO §30 (Brandwände) and §29 (Trennwände): Gebäudeabschlusswände and internal Brandwände are required to subdivide extensive buildings at maximum intervals of 40 m ("Gebäude ... sind in Abständen von nicht mehr als 40 m durch innere Brandwände zu unterteilen"). Brandwände are required to be fire-resistant (feuerbeständig) and made of non-combustible materials, and they must also resist mechanical loads. Under the older DIN 4102, Brandwand = F 90-A plus mechanical impact resistance. The question's options give "40 m; F 90-A" as B.

question.text: Under German building regulations, (a) what fire resistance class must corridor walls have when they are the side walls of escape routes, and (b) if lighting openings with G-glazing are installed in such walls, what minimum height above floor level must the lower edge of the glass be?
source: A typical area of application for G-glazing is the openings for lighting installed in corridor walls, which have to be constructed fire-retarding (F 30) as the side walls of escape routes. The lower edge of the glass must in this case be at least 1.80 m above floor level, so that in case of fire the corridor remains usable in the radiation shadow.
context:
Scope of application
Under building regulations, G-glazing may be installed only where there are no higher requirements for fire protection reasons. A typical area of application for G-glazing is the openings for lighting installed in corridor walls, which have to be constructed fire-retarding (F 30) as the side walls of escape routes. The lower edge of the glass must in this case be at least 1.80 m above floor level, so that in case of fire the corridor remains usable in the radiation shadow.

Construction
Classified materials for the construction of conventional massive load-bearing or non-load-bearing walls are shown in → 8. Steel columns and steel supporting beams are today normally fitted with box-shaped claddings of fire protection boards, whose thickness depends on the profile dimensions and the required fire resistance class → 1 – 3. There are also non-foaming coatings (to F 90) and composite constructions with concrete filling, if necessary with additional reinforcement (F 60). Non-load-bearing separating walls can be constructed as stud partitions of various qualities → 4 – 6.

answer.text:
This looks like it comes from Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre. In the section on corridors and escape routes (Flure), the text says corridor walls must be F 30 and fire-retardant (feuerhemmend). It also says lighting openings (Lichtöffnungen) with G-glazing are permitted in these walls if the lower edge is at least 1.80 m above the floor. I'm recalling this rather than deriving it.

The German model building regulations (MBO) do allow "notwendige Flure" to have walls of F 30 fire resistance, and in the older rules, openings in corridor walls had to be fire-resistant glazing (G).

The 1.80 m figure is the one I associate with this rule. The 1.20 m figure may relate to something else, such as parapet heights.

Answer: B

question.text: Under German building regulations (general rule, not the high-rise guideline), legally essential escape-route corridors longer than what length must be divided by self-closing, smoke-proof closures?

context: Closures between stairways and corridors legally essential as escape routes and also for the division of legally essential corridors more than 30 m long must be self-closing and smoke-proof → p. 511.

answer.text:
Under the Musterbauordnung (MBO) and the Muster-Verwaltungsvorschrift, and under state building codes such as the BauO NRW, § 36 (Notwendige Flure) requires that notwendige Flure longer than 30 m be divided by rauchdichte und selbstschließende Abschlüsse into sections no longer than 30 m. The wording is "Notwendige Flure sind durch nichtabschließbare, rauchdichte und selbstschließende Abschlüsse in Rauchabschnitte zu unterteilen. Die Rauchabschnitte sollen nicht länger als 30 m sein."

This applies to the general rule, not the high-rise guideline.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In dwelling design, which compass orientation should the kitchen ideally have?
source: The location of the kitchen is ideally on the northeast or northwest
context:
Location
The location of the kitchen is ideally on the northeast or northwest, in the immediate vicinity of the entrance area (short distances for shopping, rubbish etc.), to the (vegetable) garden and the cellar. There should be sensible internal room relationships with the dining room, utility room and larder. It should ideally be possible to see the front door, children’s play area and terrace from the kitchen → ④.

answer.text:
In German design guidance (e.g., Neufert), the kitchen is ideally oriented to the north or east, which keeps it cool and spares it the afternoon sun. Neufert's orientation guidance for dwellings gives bedrooms to the east, living rooms to the south and west, and kitchens to the north, northeast or east. Among the options, northeast or northwest comes closest to the north-facing ideal. Option B, east or southeast, is also plausible, since morning sun suits a kitchen.

The more precise Neufert wording is "Küche: Nordost bis Nordwest" for a cool location. Option D matches that range, so I choose D.

Answer: D

question.text: Under German building regulations, if a window serves as an escape route, what minimum clear opening (width × height) must it have, and what maximum sill height above floor level?
source: If the window serves as an escape route, it must have a clear opening of at least 0.9 × 1.2 m and a sill height of max. 1.2 m above floor level.
context:

How far do the casements open into the room? Is the window sill still usable when the window is open? (Tilted windows are not sufficient for through ventilation! They ensure only the slow cooling of a room.) There may also be specific requirements for fire protection or for resistance against break-in or damage. Resistance classes → pp. 107, 118. If the window serves as an escape route, it must have a clear opening of at least 0.9 × 1.2 m and a sill height of max. 1.2 m above floor level.

answer.text:
German building regulations (the Landesbauordnungen, e.g. MBO § 35 and the Arbeitsstättenrichtlinie) set requirements for windows used as emergency exits and rescue openings.

Under the MBO, a window used as a rescue opening for the fire brigade must have a clear opening of at least 0.9 m × 1.2 m. For residential rooms, the minimum is 0.6 m × 1.0 m, with a sill height of no more than 1.2 m. The requirement for 0.9 × 1.2 applies to openings in the second escape route, and the sill height is also given as 1.2 m.

The question asks about a window serving as an escape route. Option A (0.6 × 1.0 m; 1.2 m) matches the MBO residential rescue opening rule: "mindestens 0,90 m × 1,20 m" for a rescue opening, with the lower value of 0.6 × 1.0 m applying to windows in residential buildings (§ 33 MBO, Rettungswege). Option C (0.9 × 1.2 m; 1.2 m) matches the larger dimensions and could fit another reading of the rule. Under MBO § 33, a window serving as a rescue opening must have a clear opening of at least 0.9 m × 1.2 m, and the sill must not be higher than 1.2 m. The 0.6 × 1.0 m dimensions come from § 35 of the Muster-Bauordnung for the rescue of people via emergency windows, which is the version where the opening is 0.6 × 1.0 m and the sill 1.2 m.

For a window that serves as an escape route, the common rule cited is 0.9 × 1.2 m. The 0.6 × 1.0 m / 1.2 m figures are those used in the Landesbauordnungen for rescue openings of rooms in residential buildings, and these are the widely cited ones (e.g. "Fenster als Rettungsweg: mind. 0,60 × 1,00 m, Brüstungshöhe max. 1,20 m"). The 0.9 × 1.2 m figure applies to rescue openings used by the fire service with rescue equipment (Fenster für die Rettung, Notausstieg in Arbeitsstätten).

Because the question speaks of an escape route in general building regulations, I take the commonly cited 0.6 × 1.0 m with sill height 1.2 m.

Answer: A

The German Arbeitsstättenrichtlinie ASR A3.4 (and the earlier ASR 7/1) addresses the visual connection to the outside. Under the older rule in ASR 7/1, the sum of the widths of the visual connections had to be at least 1/10 of the sum of all the room's wall widths (the room perimeter). I recall the wording as: "the total width of the visual connections should be at least 1/10 of the sum of all wall widths, the room's width/perimeter." Neufert quotes this as: "Die Summe der Sichtverbindungsbreiten soll mindestens 1/10 der Summe aller Wandbreiten des Raumes betragen." Further related requirements: the glazed area must be at least 1/8 of the room floor area, and the minimum window width is 1 m.

Under the German Muster-Hochhaus-Richtlinie (MHHR) and the Landesbauordnungen, exterior walls in a high-rise must prevent fire from spreading over the façade to other storeys. question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In residential design, under what condition are kitchens and kitchenettes without windows permissible?

Always, provided artificial lighting is installed

answer.text:
In German practice (Neufert and the state building codes), kitchens and kitchenettes without windows are permitted if effective ventilation is ensured, for example through mechanical extraction. The usual wording is that windowless kitchens are only allowed with effective ventilation, so A fits.

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In side-lit industrial/work buildings, the distance of the working area from the window should be what multiple of the clear window height?

Lighting
Multi-storey buildings with windows on one side should face northeast, and, with windows on both sides facing north and south, they should be oriented east–west. Some sources give 3 times for industrial buildings, but the 2 times figure matches the phrasing of the question best.

question.text: For escape routes in high-rise buildings under German regulations, what are (a) the minimum width of escape routes, (b) the maximum walking distance from any point in an occupied room, and (c) the maximum length of a branch corridor with only one escape direction when no second escape route is available?
source: Escape routes are min. 1.25 m wide and should if possible lead in two directions, to each staircase. The maximum walking distance from each point of an occupied room may not exceed 25 m. Corridors with two escape directions may be max. 40 m long. After 20 m, a smoke-proof self-closing door must be installed. Branch corridors with only one escape direction may be max. 10 m long. If a second escape route (e.g. an escape balcony) is available, max. 20 m.
context:
Escape routes
Escape routes are min. 1.25 m wide and should if possible lead in two directions, to each staircase. The maximum walking distance from each point of an occupied room may not exceed 25 m. Corridors with two escape directions may be max. 40 m long. After 20 m, a smoke-proof self-closing door must be installed. Branch corridors with only one escape direction may be max. 10 m long. If a second escape route (e.g. an escape balcony) is available, max. 20 m.

answer.text:
The German High-Rise Guideline (Muster-Hochhausrichtlinie, MHHR) and typical building regulations set these values:

- Under the MBO, the walking distance to a stairwell or exit from any point in an occupied room is at most 35 m (the high-rise guideline uses the same 35 m).
- Under the MHHR, the minimum width of escape routes (corridors) is 1.25 m.
- Dead-end corridors are limited to 15 m under the MHHR. That is the length of a corridor with only one escape direction.

I'm recalling this from memory. The MHHR (2012) states in Section 6 that the walking distance from any point in an occupied room to a safety stairwell must not exceed 35 m. It also states that corridors in high-rises have a minimum clear width of 1.25 m, and that the length of a dead-end corridor must not exceed 15 m. The MBO's general dead-end limit is 15 m for corridors, which fits.

So the two figures I'm confident in are 1.25 m and 35 m. The options with 1.25 m and 35 m are C and D's variants, and only C has 1.25 m with 35 m, giving a dead-end length of 20 m. D has 1.20 m, which doesn't match my recollection of 1.25 m.

Option C's 20 m dead-end value is the one that conflicts with my memory of 15 m. My recollection of the 15 m dead-end limit is less certain than the 1.25 m width, and the MHHR does specify "Stichflure bis 20 m" in some versions. Since C is the only option with both 1.25 m and 35 m, I'll go with it.

Answer: C

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Single-leaf external masonry walls without an additional insulation layer must meet high thermal insulation requirements. What materials does this restrict their construction to?
options: Highly insulating blocks (e.g. aerated blocks) with special thermally insulating mortar and plaster
Dense solid clay bricks with standard mortar and lime plaster
Any masonry unit, provided a mesh-reinforced render is applied
source: Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.
context:
External wall construction
Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters. If the blocks used are susceptible to frost damage, they have to be rendered or protected in other ways. If the masonry is externally visible, then each course must consist of at least two rows of blocks of the same height with a continuous 20 mm thick longitudinal joint between them, and each course staggered and mortared without voids.
Single-leaf walls with additional insulation layers → ③ – ⑥ (external, internal insulation → Building physics, p. 471 ff.) are therefore a common alternative.

On the external side of the insulating layers, there is a risk of cracking due to heat build-up and substrate with poor shear strength, so mineral render reinforced with mesh is used here (or plastic modified render).

External wall construction
Single-leaf external walls → ① – ② are unproblematic regarding building physics, but on account of the high thermal insulation requirements can only be built with materials with high thermal insulation value (e.g. aerated blocks) and special thermally insulated mortars and plasters. If the blocks used are susceptible to frost damage, they have to be rendered or protected in other ways. If the masonry is externally visible, then each course must consist of at least two rows of blocks of the same height with a continuous 20 mm thick longitudinal joint between them, and each course staggered and mortared without voids.

meta.title: 单层外墙与附加保温层

answer.text:
Single-leaf external masonry without added insulation (monolithic walls) has to meet the thermal requirements through the wall material alone. That limits construction to highly insulating blocks such as aerated concrete, lightweight concrete or high-porosity perforated clay blocks. These are typically laid with thin-bed or lightweight mortar and finished with thermally insulating plaster. Dense solid bricks, calcium-silicate blocks and arbitrary units cannot reach the required U-values.

Answer: A

A slight fixed roof overhang is sufficient

answer.text:
This appears to come from Neufert's Architects' Data or a similar reference on office buildings, which draws on Rosenauer. The question is which orientation is typical for US offices and why.

East–west façades get low morning and evening sun, which is hard to shade and causes glare. A north–south main axis puts the long façades facing east and west, so the building takes in that low sun. An east–west main axis puts the long façades facing north and south. The south façade is easy to shade with horizontal overhangs, and the north façade gets no direct sun. So a main axis running east–west is the preferred orientation.

That narrows it to B or D. The statement that the low morning and evening sun is disturbing matches the reasoning in the source, which says the main axis is east–west so that the low east and west sun does not disturb. Option D's reason, maximising winter gains, is less likely to be what Rosenauer gave.

Answer: B

meta.title: 视野：窗宽不小于房间宽 65%

answer.text:
I recall that in Neufert's Bauentwurfslehre, the guidance on daylighting and views out says the window area should be at least 1/8 of the floor area, according to the Landesbauordnung (state building codes). The rules from DIN 5034 and Neufert also give figures for the window width relative to the room width.

Neufert states that for a sufficient view out, the window width should be at least 55% of the room width, and that the height of the parapet should not exceed 0.9 m. On the other hand, according to DIN 5034-4 the window width should be at least 55% of the room width, and a window width of at least 30% of the room width is also mentioned. The text from DIN 5034-1 reads: "Die Fensterbreite soll mindestens 55 % der Raumbreite betragen." The options here are 80, 50, 40 and 65. Under the DIN 5034 rule of the "Sichtverbindung nach außen", the minimum values are given by the width of the window in the raw structure (Rohbaumaß): 
- Window width ≥ 55% of the room width, 
- Height of the clear view ≥ 1.25 m, 
- Sill height ≤ 0.95 m.

Since 55% is not among the options, I need the closest. In DIN EN 17037, the horizontal view angle is at least 14° and the same requirement also comes with the width of the window. In the older DIN 5034-1 (1983), the minimum window width was given as 55% of the room width, and the rule that "Die Summe der Fensterbreiten sollte mindestens ein Drittel der Raumbreite betragen" was also given. I am not sure of the exact figure from the other source, but a rule of 55% would be closest to 50%.

I'll go with 50%.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: How is the thermal resistance R of a single building layer calculated, and how is the overall resistance 1/U of a building element composed?
options: R = d·λ; U = R_si + R + R_se
source: Thermal resistance R, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal] is a property of a layer: R = d/λ (d = layer thickness in m).

Overall resistance 1/U, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal], is the sum of the resistances of a building element to the transmission of heat (thermal resistances and surface resistances): 1/U = R_{si} + R + R_{se}
context: Thermal resistance R, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal] is a property of a layer: R = d/λ (d = layer thickness in m). The calculation of the thermal resistance is important for the determination of the heat transfer coefficient U → ③ – ④.

Overall resistance 1/U, unit m^2K/W [m^2hK/kcal], is the sum of the resistances of a building element to the transmission of heat (thermal resistances and surface resistances): 1/U = R_{si} + R + R_{se}

But in example → ⑤ condensation is formed on the inner face of the building element, because the proportion of the surface air film is too large. The surface air film cannot exceed a certain proportion X of the overall resistance 1/U → ③.

answer.text:
The thermal resistance of a single layer is R = d/λ, with thickness d in m and thermal conductivity λ in W/(m·K). The total resistance of the element is the sum of the layer resistances plus the internal and external surface resistances: R_T = 1/U = R_si + ΣR + R_se.

Checking the options: A inverts the layer formula, B uses a product and sets U equal to a resistance sum, and D subtracts the surface resistances. Only C matches.

Answer: C

meta.title: 混凝土外墙必须附加保温

answer.text:
Under the German Energy Saving Ordinance (EnEV, now GEG) and DIN 4108, a solid concrete wall has a high thermal conductivity (about 2.0 W/mK for normal-weight concrete). Even a 30 cm wall would have a U-value of roughly 3 W/m²K, far above the permitted maximum. It would also create significant thermal bridges and condensation risk. Normal concrete therefore cannot satisfy the requirements without extra insulation.

Options A, B and C each rest on a condition (building class, thickness, pre-casting) that does not change this. Insulation-free exterior walls are possible only with lightweight concrete or other special materials, and that is not what a solid concrete wall means here.

The best answer is D.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: To avoid condensation within a building element, on which side must the vapour barrier be installed?
options: In the middle of the insulation layer
In the ventilated cavity outside the insulation
source: If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side
context:
Construction with vapour barrier → 3 – 4
More recent building ('warm roof', 'warm façade') features an external vapour barrier layer (e.g. waterproofing) and, on account of this, an additional internal vapour barrier. In order to prevent condensation on the inside face of the building element, the layers in front of the vapour barrier cannot exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance → p. 472. Warm façades require careful construction and have therefore mostly become established as prefabricated systems (sandwich construction). In a warm roof, a water vapour pressure equalisation layer is arranged under the waterproofing, and only an equalisation layer for the damping of stresses is provided under the vapour barrier.

Vapour barrier at the correct location
If there is a vapour barrier on the outside, then the entire vapour pressure gradient occurs there and the result is condensation → 8; if this is to be avoided, then a vapour barrier must be installed on the warm side with an equivalent diffusion resistance suitable for the location, in which case the layers in front of the vapour barrier must not exceed a certain proportion of the overall thermal resistance 1/U → 9.

The vapour barrier is under the thermal insulation to prevent condensation inside the roof construction. When the vapour barrier is installed, it is important that all air flow between interior and roof construction is prevented. Any penetration points, laps and junctions with building elements must be carefully sealed. Inner cladding is normally plasterboard on support construction (pay attention to the possibility of cracks!).

answer.text:
A vapour barrier (Dampfsperre) belongs on the warm side of the insulation, which in winter is the interior side. This stops warm, moist indoor air from diffusing into the construction and condensing in the colder layers. That matches DIN 4108 practice.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In an 'upside-down' (inverted) flat roof, how are the waterproofing, vapour barrier and insulation arranged?
options: Waterproofing/vapour barrier as one layer on the structure, closed-cell insulation loose on top, gravel
Insulation on the underside of the slab, waterproofing on top of the slab
Vapour barrier on the structure, insulation above, waterproofing on top of the insulation
Ventilated cavity between two insulation layers, waterproofing on top
source: or an 'upside-down roof' → 8 (waterproofing and vapour barrier are applied as one layer directly onto the load-bearing construction and the closed-cell insulation is loosely laid on top and secured with a gravel layer)
context: Non-ventilated, single-layer construction ('warm roof'), in which the load-bearing structure, vapour barrier, thermal insulation and waterproofing (including intermediate layers) form a composite element.

This can either be the conventional construction → 10, or an 'upside-down roof' → 8 (waterproofing and vapour barrier are applied as one layer directly onto the load-bearing construction and the closed-cell insulation is loosely laid on top and secured with a gravel layer), or a combination of both construction types (e.g. a 'plus roof'), or with internal insulation → 9.

meta.title: 平屋面构造：暖屋面与倒置屋面

answer.text:
An inverted roof (Umkehrdach) has the waterproofing directly on the structure, which also acts as the vapour barrier. Closed-cell insulation (XPS) is laid loose on top of it, and a ballast layer of gravel or paving goes over that, often with a separating or filter fleece between the insulation and the ballast.

Option A matches this. The other options do not:
- B places the insulation under the slab, which is not an inverted roof.
- C describes a conventional warm roof.
- D describes a ventilated cold roof.

Answer: A

question.text: In German masonry construction, for a two-leaf cavity wall with a non-load-bearing outer weather-protection leaf, what is the minimum thickness of the outer leaf, and what are the minimum and maximum widths of the air gap?
source: Cavity walls consist of an inner load-bearing wall and an outer non-load-bearing weather protection facing (minimum thickness 90 mm). They can be built with an air gap, with air gap and thermal insulation, with cavity-filling insulation and with intermediate plaster layer
The width of the air gap should be min. 40 mm (max. 150 mm).
context: Cavity walls consist of an inner load-bearing wall and an outer non-load-bearing weather protection facing (minimum thickness 90 mm). They can be built with an air gap, with air gap and thermal insulation, with cavity-filling insulation and with intermediate plaster layer → 7 – 10. The masonry leaves are connected with ties of non-rusting steel. The width of the air gap should be min. 40 mm (max. 150 mm). Vertical expansion joints should be provided in the external leaf and there should also be ventilation openings (e.g. open vertical joints) at the top and bottom, with the openings at the bottom also serving to drain water p. 77 → 3.

Cavity walls consist of an inner load-bearing wall and an outer non-load-bearing weather protection facing (minimum thickness 90 mm). They can be built with an air gap, with air gap and thermal insulation, with cavity-filling insulation and with intermediate plaster layer → 7 – 10. The masonry leaves are connected with ties of non-rusting steel. The width of the air gap should be min. 40 mm (max. 150 mm). Vertical expansion joints should be provided in the external leaf and there should also be ventilation openings (e.g. open vertical joints) at the top and bottom, with the openings at the bottom also serving to drain water p. 77 → 3.

meta.title: 夹心墙（双叶墙）的外叶与空气层

answer.text:
Under DIN 1053-1 (and DIN EN 1996), the outer leaf of a two-leaf cavity wall (Hohlschichtmauerwerk / zweischaliges Mauerwerk with air gap) must be at least 90 mm thick. The air gap is normally 60 to 150 mm, or 40 mm minimum if the gap is fully filled with mortar-free mortar and leaf is built... Specifically: DIN 1053-1 says the air gap should be at least 60 mm wide, and it may be reduced to 40 mm if the mortar is struck off smooth on the inside of the joint. The maximum width is 150 mm, unless proof is given for larger ties.

Option B says 90 mm outer leaf with a 40–150 mm air gap, which matches the 40 mm minimum (with the reduced requirement) and 150 mm maximum. The other options fail on the outer leaf thickness or the gap range.

The standard text states: "Die Mindestdicke der Außenschale beträgt 90 mm. Der Schalenabstand darf maximal 150 mm betragen. Mindestens 60 mm Luftschicht, bei Verfüllung der Fugen 40 mm."

B is the best match.

Answer: B

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: What minimum slope should a flat roof generally have, and what minimum slope is recommended to allow for unavoidable flatness tolerances and deflection?
source: Flat roofs are defined as roofs with a slope of up to 5%. Flat roofs without slope are possible as a special construction in exceptional cases. Flat roofs should generally have a minimum slope of 2%.
it is recommended to construct flat roofs with a minimum slope of 5% (3°).
context: Flat roofs are defined as roofs with a slope of up to 5%. Flat roofs without slope are possible as a special construction in exceptional cases. Flat roofs should generally have a minimum slope of 2%. On account of unavoidable flatness tolerances and deflection of the construction, however, it is recommended to construct flat roofs with a minimum slope of 5% (3°).

Flat roofs are defined as roofs with a slope of up to 5%. Flat roofs without slope are possible as a special construction in exceptional cases. Flat roofs should generally have a minimum slope of 2%. On account of unavoidable flatness tolerances and deflection of the construction, however, it is recommended to construct flat roofs with a minimum slope of 5% (3°).

answer.text:
In German practice, DIN 18531 and the flat roof guidelines (Flachdachrichtlinie) set the figures. Roofs with a slope of less than 5% are treated as special cases that need extra measures. Older versions of the guidelines required a minimum slope of 2% (about 1.1°), and recommended 5% (3°) so that unavoidable tolerances and deflection do not create ponding.

Of the options, 2% / 5% (3°) matches this: 5% is roughly 2.9°, which fits the "3°" label.

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: Compared with a poorly insulated building envelope, how severe are the consequences of a thermal bridge in a highly insulated envelope?
options: Less severe, because overall heat loss is lower
About the same; insulation level is irrelevant
Negligible once U-values are low enough
source: Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas.
Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation.
context:
Thermal bridge
Thermal bridges are parts of building elements with low thermal insulation compared with surrounding areas. This results in the proportion of the surface air film in the overall resistance increasing so that the surface temperature of the inner side of the thermal bridge sinks and condensation forms.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. Thermal bridges can be considered, according to EnEV, for the determination of the annual heating energy demand by increasing the thermal transmission values (U-values) or in a separate verification.

Good thermal insulation includes not only highly insulated building components, but also the appropriate connections between the building elements. There is a danger of additional heat loss at these joints and low surface temperature in the building elements during the heating period. Additional consumption of energy for heating and the possibility of condensation and mould formation are the result. Thus it should be borne in mind that this thermal bridging effect can have considerably worse consequences with highly insulated elements than with building elements with less thermal insulation. Thermal bridges can be considered, according to EnEV, for the determination of the annual heating energy demand by increasing the thermal transmission values (U-values) or in a separate verification.

answer.text:
In a highly insulated envelope, a thermal bridge makes up a much larger share of total heat loss. The surface temperature at the thermal bridge also falls well below that of the surrounding insulated surfaces, so the risk of condensation and mold is greater. Thermal bridges therefore matter more in well-insulated buildings, and DIN 4108 Beiblatt 2 and the Passivhaus approach aim for thermal-bridge-free design for this reason.

The consequences are considerably worse, which is option D.

Answer: D

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: In external walls with a rear-ventilated outer skin, what minimum air-gap width is required behind a panel-like outer skin, and behind a brickwork outer skin?
source: The rear ventilation of the skin removes the vapour barrier effect of the relatively vapour-sealed outer layers. The width of the air gap with panel-like external skin amounts to min. 20 mm, or for brickwork outer skin min. 40 mm.
context:
Construction with rear-ventilated outer skin → ⑤ – ⑥
The rear ventilation of the skin removes the vapour barrier effect of the relatively vapour-sealed outer layers. The width of the air gap with panel-like external skin amounts to min. 20 mm, or for brickwork outer skin min. 40 mm.

meta.title: 背通风外挂层的空气间层

answer.text:
The relevant rule is DIN 1053-1 for brickwork and DIN 18516-1 for rear-ventilated cladding panels.

For a rear-ventilated outer skin (Vorhangfassade) under DIN 18516-1, the minimum ventilation gap is 20 mm. Local reductions down to 5 mm are permitted at some points, for example at substructures. For two-leaf masonry with an air layer (Verblendschale) under DIN 1053-1, the air layer is typically 40 mm minimum, and 60 mm if mortar residue is not removed. So the "40 mm for brickwork" figure is the standard one when the air gap is combined with thermal insulation. The stated figures in the Neufert-style rule are 20 mm for panels and 40 mm for brickwork.

Option D gives 40 mm for panels, which does not match the 20 mm rule. Option A matches the figures above.

Answer: A

question.text: In German (DIN-based) design practice: For a fixed horizontal sun-shading projection above a window, which formula gives the projection A in terms of the shadow angle α and the window height H (and the minimum projection when wall thickness D is taken into account)?
options: A = tan α × H; minimum A = (tan α × H) − D
A = sin α × H; minimum A = sin α × H + D
A = tan α × H + D; minimum A = tan α × H
A = H / tan α; minimum A = H / tan α − D
source: Projection A = tan shadow angle \( \alpha 	imes \) window height H;
but min. projection A = (tan shadow angle \( \alpha 	imes \) window height H) – wall thickness D

answer.text:
This looks like the Neufert-style formula for a fixed horizontal overhang (Sonnenschutz). The shadow angle α is measured from the horizontal, so the shadow cast by a projection A reaches a depth of A × tan α on the wall below, assuming α is defined as the angle between the sun's rays and the horizontal. If instead α is measured from the vertical, the relationship changes.

The aim is for the shadow to cover the window height H. Taking α as the vertical shadow angle, the shadow on the wall falls A / tan α below the overhang, or A × tan α if α is measured from the vertical. Since the question lists A = tan α × H, I'll assume that form.

Whether the wall thickness D is added or subtracted depends on where the window sits. If the window is set back in the wall by D, the wall's own reveal already provides some shading. The overhang measured from the wall face then only needs to be A − D, so the minimum projection is (tan α × H) − D. That corresponds to option A.

Option C gives A = tan α × H + D as the main formula, which doesn't fit the idea that the thickness reduces the needed projection. Option A is consistent with the reveal reducing it.

Answer: A

source: The units of the modular system are the basic module M = 100 mm and the multi-modules 3 M = 300 mm, 6 M = 600 mm and 12 M = 1200 mm.

There are also standardised non-modular supplementary dimensions l = 25 mm, 50 mm and 75 mm for fitting elements or overlapping connections → 11. Combination rules can be used to fit building components of various sizes into a modular coordinate system.
